values: Methods description — MVA Hackathon 2026, Track 1 (Variant Prediction)

Please submit your answers with your Track 1 submission. All questions (with the exception of Question 1, in red) are voluntary; however, submissions without a methods description may be judged less favorably on the Innovation and Scalability criteria, since the panel can't assess what it can't see.

Fill out this form once per model/approach submitted.
Answers
Team name
Mame Diarra Toure and Bonaventure Dossou
Model number (fill out this form once per model/approach submitted; up to 6)
Model 1: genome-wide candidate generation with the selected wide rank-50 SBNN ranker
Please describe your model/approach in detail.

The approach has two linked parts. Bonaventure Dossou's genome workflow processes the gated child data, checks the GRCh38 representation and read evidence, normalizes the supplied VCF, joins functional annotations, evaluates rarity and predicted consequence, phases heterozygous alleles where reads permit, matches the HPO phenotype, and constructs inheritance-compatible same-gene pairs. The strict filter requires PASS calls, depth at least 10, genotype quality at least 20, heterozygous allele balance from 0.20 to 0.80, population allele frequency no greater than 0.005 when observed, and no direct cis evidence. This reduced 5.08 million variants to six reportable compound-heterozygous pairs. Mame Diarra Toure developed the learned ranking extension. The selected model is a 50-200-100-1 Singular Bayesian Neural Network with ranks (50,50,1), KL weight 0.01, posterior scale multiplier 0.1, and prior scale 0.3. It was trained on ClinVar 2023 pathogenic versus benign labels with gene-disjoint validation and tested on ClinVar variants absent from the 2023 snapshot. For the child, 128 posterior weight samples produce each allele probability. A pair receives sqrt(P1 x P2) x HPO phenotype similarity. The challenge answer, previous rank, submitted pair score, ClinVar significance, CADD, REVEL, SpliceAI, and disease name were excluded from this transfer adapter. generate_track1_submission.py runs the fitted suite and exports the selected wide-rank SBNN result. Hugging Face accepted that CSV as Submission 2 for PROBAND01, with a full match at rank 1, 100 Rank Points, F-max 1.000, and an F-max EPCR threshold of 0.3724070924857989.

(required) If commercially-available Generative AI was used, record the provider, the plan or tier, and the relevant setting in your methods description. A line is enough, for example, "Anthropic API, Claude Sonnet, commercial terms, no training on customer content."

OpenAI Codex was used for code assistance, testing, analysis, and drafting. The account plan or tier was not recorded in the project files. Private FASTQ and full VCF data were not uploaded to the model.
Please state whether the submission file is the automated output of your computational approach (preferred), or if it has undergone downstream manual review and curation.

The submitted CSV is automated output. generate_track1_submission.py loads the retained model checkpoint, calls verify_temporal_models_track1.py for posterior inference and pair scoring, selects strict_wide_rank50_sbnn.csv, and calls export_track1_sbnn_submission.py for schema and score validation. No row was manually inserted, deleted, or reordered after model inference.
Please describe any downstream manual review in detail.

Manual review was limited to quality assurance and interpretation. The team checked reference build, variant representation, read quality, population frequency, consequence, phenotype fit, phase evidence, gene-disease validity, output schema, and the reproduced public evaluator. This review identified unresolved phase and functional uncertainty for p.Asn1002Lys but did not alter the automated SBNN ordering or EPCR values.

Please state whether your approach only used publicly available data (preferred) or if proprietary data was also used. If proprietary data were used, where possible, please also include a submission based only on publicly available data.

External training, validation, and reference resources were publicly available. The child's approximately 85 GB WGS and phenotype bundle was gated challenge data supplied by SageBio under the hackathon access terms. No commercial proprietary annotation database or private external patient cohort was used.
Please describe any public data used in detail (e.g., reference panels, population databases, literature).

Public resources included ClinVar GRCh38 snapshots from 26 December 2023 and 29 August 2026 for temporal training and testing; gnomAD population frequencies; CADD, REVEL, and SpliceAI annotations through OpenCRAVAT; Human Phenotype Ontology release 9 October 2023; Phenopacket Store release 0.1.27 for solved-patient ranking experiments; and peer-reviewed BUB1B, Bayesian neural-network, and rare-disease prioritization literature. Sources: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/clinvar/docs/downloads/ ; https://gnomad.broadinstitute.org/ ; https://hpo.jax.org/ ; https://github.com/monarch-initiative/phenopacket-store/releases/tag/0.1.27
Please describe any proprietary data used in detail.

No proprietary training or reference database was used. The only non-public input was the gated child WGS and phenotype bundle supplied by SageBio for this challenge. The raw patient files remain on controlled cluster storage and are not distributed in the repository.
Is your approach able to output proposed pairs of compound heterozygous candidate variants, or only single candidate variants?

The approach explicitly outputs compound-heterozygous candidate pairs. It constructs pairs from two heterozygous alleles in the same gene, removes pairs with direct cis evidence, records trans-read-backed or unknown phase, and scores both alleles jointly. The final Track 1 file contains six paired hypotheses and ranks the BUB1B pair first.
How did you handle secondary or incidental findings, if any? (See the finding_type column in your submission.)

Only primary causal findings were submitted. Every row has finding_type=primary. The project did not perform or report a systematic secondary or incidental finding analysis, and no candidate was promoted as an incidental finding.
Please provide an estimate of run time and cost for your approach (if possible).

Checkpoint inference and generation of all strict and broad candidate CSVs completes in under one minute on the recorded Apple M2 CPU; the measured local rerun took only a few seconds and had no marginal cloud cost. The WGS alignment and annotation ran on Mila cluster CPU storage, but a reliable end-to-end wall-clock and accounting cost were not retained. Full temporal retraining and the joint hyperparameter sweeps are separate research runs and are not required to regenerate the submission.
Provide a method abstract (up to 500 words). Please include strengths and limitations of your method as well as methodological detail.

We developed a genome-to-ranking workflow for the Rare Disease, Real Kid Track 1 task. Bonaventure Dossou's upstream pipeline aligned and checked read evidence, normalized and annotated 5.08 million supplied variants, applied quality, rarity, consequence, inheritance, phase, and HPO filters, and produced six reportable compound-heterozygous hypotheses. Mame Diarra Toure developed the probabilistic ranking and external evaluation. The submitted model is a 50-200-100-1 low-rank Singular Bayesian Neural Network with ranks (50,50,1). Its factorized weight posterior scales with rank times the sum of the layer widths rather than the full dense weight matrix, providing a practical path to wider Bayesian models with lower parameter and optimizer-state memory. It was trained on ClinVar 2023 pathogenic versus benign variants and selected using validation data that were separate from the final temporal holdout. For each child candidate pair, 128 posterior samples estimate two allele probabilities, which are combined by their geometric mean and the upstream phenotype similarity. The final CSV is produced automatically by generate_track1_submission.py and ranks the accepted BUB1B pair first. The live Hugging Face evaluator accepted it as Submission 2 for PROBAND01 and returned a full match at rank 1, 100 Rank Points, F-max 1.000, and an F-max EPCR threshold of 0.3724070924857989. This exactly matches the independent local evaluation. The main strength is the separation of biological candidate validity from learned ranking, followed by temporal and patient-level tests rather than relying on one solved child. On the untouched temporal ClinVar holdout, the selected SBNN reached 84.35% top-1, PR-AUC 0.9736, and F-max 0.9235. HPO conditioning improved ranking on 719 post-2023 solved Phenopacket cases. Limitations remain important: the external patient benchmark uses constructed ten-candidate sets rather than complete exomes; the two BUB1B alleles are not directly phased in trans; p.Asn1002Lys lacks functional confirmation; and SBNN uncertainty was weaker for unseen-gene detection than a five-network deep ensemble. The method is a research prioritization system, not a validated clinical diagnostic device.

values: Methods description — MVA Hackathon 2026, Track 2 (Drug Repurposing)

Please submit your answers with your Track 2 report. All questions (with the exception of Question 1, in red) are voluntary; however, submissions without a methods description may be judged less favorably on the Scientific Rigor and Innovation criteria, since the panel can't assess what it can't see.

Track 2 accepts one final submission per team.
Answers
Team name
Mame Diarra Toure and Bonaventure Dossou
Please describe your approach in detail (how you went from variant/mechanism to candidate medication(s)).

Track 2 starts from the Track 1 BUB1B compound-heterozygous hypothesis. The p.Leu737Ter allele is a strong loss-of-function anchor, while p.Asn1002Lys may alter BUBR1 abundance, localization, or checkpoint activity but remains functionally untested. The working mechanism is reduced BUBR1 function, weakened spindle-assembly checkpoint control, chromosome-segregation errors, and mosaic aneuploidy. Candidate identification therefore focused on mechanism rescue rather than disease-name matching. The principal experimental lead is the NAD+/SIRT2/BUBR1 stabilization axis: published work reports SIRT2-mediated BUBR1 stabilization and increased BUBR1 abundance after nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN) treatment in a mouse context. The BUBR1/PP2A-B56/Aurora B balance provides a second assayable pathway, not a treatment claim. The proposal first validates the patient's cellular defect in patient-derived cells with a CRISPR-corrected isogenic control and BUB1B add-back control. A compound and dose screen then measures BUBR1 abundance and localization, mitotic timing after spindle perturbation, lagging chromosomes, micronuclei, premature chromatid separation, viability, proliferation, and DNA-damage signals. A Bayesian hierarchical dose-response model estimates the posterior probability of multi-endpoint rescue without unacceptable toxicity and selects follow-up compound-dose combinations by expected information gain.

(required) If commercially-available Generative AI was used, record the provider, the plan or tier, and the relevant setting in your methods description. A line is enough, for example, "Anthropic API, Claude Sonnet, commercial terms, no training on customer content."

OpenAI Codex was used for code assistance, literature organization, analysis, and drafting. The account plan or tier was not recorded in the project files. Private FASTQ and full VCF data were not uploaded to the model.
Was candidate identification automated (e.g., via a drug-target database query or LLM-assisted search), or primarily manual literature review and expert curation?

Candidate identification was primarily mechanism-driven manual literature review and expert curation. No automated drug-target ranking system produced the candidate. The computational component is a proposed Bayesian design and analysis framework for a future cell-based compound and dose screen; that experiment has not yet been run.
Please describe any manual literature review or expert curation in detail.

The review followed the causal chain from biallelic BUB1B variation to reduced BUBR1 function, spindle-checkpoint failure, chromosome mis-segregation, and MVA. The team checked peer-reviewed evidence for BUBR1 dysfunction, SIRT2-dependent BUBR1 stabilization, the reported NMN mouse result, and the BUBR1/PP2A-B56/Aurora B regulatory balance. Leads were retained only when they suggested a measurable rescue mechanism. NMN is treated as an experimental lead, not as an established treatment. Compounds that merely stop proliferation or kill aneuploid cells would be rejected.
Please state whether you relied solely on publicly available drug/target databases and literature (preferred), or whether proprietary data sources were also used.

The drug and mechanism evidence came from publicly available peer-reviewed literature and public genomic resources. The child's genotype and phenotype came from the gated SageBio challenge bundle. No proprietary drug-target database, commercial evidence platform, or private treatment-response dataset was used.
Please describe the public data sources used in detail (e.g., DrugBank, ChEMBL, ClinicalTrials.gov, OMIM, PubMed literature search).

Public sources included the original BUB1B MVA genetics paper (Nature Genetics, DOI 10.1038/ng1449), the BUBR1 dysfunction study (Cancer Research, DOI 10.1158/0008-5472.CAN-09-4319), the SIRT2/BUBR1 stabilization and NMN mouse study (EMBO Journal, DOI 10.15252/embj.201386907), and the BUBR1 pseudokinase/PP2A-B56/Aurora B study (Cell Reports, DOI 10.1016/j.celrep.2020.108397). ClinVar, gnomAD, CADD, REVEL, SpliceAI, and HPO supported interpretation of the causal variants and phenotype.
Please describe any proprietary data sources used in detail.
No proprietary drug, target, clinical-trial, or treatment-response data were used. The only restricted material was the gated child genome and phenotype supplied by SageBio for the hackathon.
How did you characterize the variant's mechanism (e.g., loss-of-function vs. gain-of-function, pathway disrupted, downstream biological consequence)?

The genotype is most consistent with partial loss of BUB1B function. p.Leu737Ter is a truncating allele expected to reduce functional BUBR1. p.Asn1002Lys is an ultra-rare missense allele with computational support but uncertain functional effect. Reduced BUBR1 weakens the spindle-assembly checkpoint and can disturb kinetochore PP2A-B56 recruitment and Aurora B balance. The downstream consequences are chromosome-alignment and segregation errors, micronuclei, and mosaic aneuploidy. The proposed assay tests whether a candidate restores BUBR1 abundance or checkpoint function and reduces segregation errors without causing nonspecific cytotoxicity.
Please provide an estimate of time or effort spent on this analysis (if possible).

A reliable person-hour log was not retained. The literature synthesis and computational assay design had negligible direct compute cost. No wet-lab screen has been performed, so experimental time and cost remain prospective and should be estimated from the selected cell model, compound library, dose grid, and replicate design.
Provide a method abstract (up to 500 words). Please include strengths and limitations of your approach as well as methodological detail.

Track 2 is framed as a testable rescue strategy for suspected biallelic BUB1B deficiency, not as an immediate treatment recommendation. The Track 1 result combines a pathogenic p.Leu737Ter allele with the ultra-rare p.Asn1002Lys allele. The working mechanism is reduced BUBR1 abundance or activity, impaired spindle-assembly-checkpoint control, chromosome-segregation errors, and mosaic aneuploidy. Literature review identified the NAD+/SIRT2/BUBR1 stabilization axis as the principal experimental lead. SIRT2-mediated deacetylation can stabilize BUBR1, and NMN increased BUBR1 abundance in a mouse context. The BUBR1/PP2A-B56/Aurora B balance supplies a second mechanistic axis and assay control. Neither result establishes an approved therapy for constitutional BUB1B deficiency. The proposed next step is a patient-derived cell assay with CRISPR-corrected isogenic and BUB1B add-back controls. Candidate compounds and doses would be evaluated on BUBR1 abundance and localization, mitotic timing after spindle perturbation, lagging chromosomes, micronuclei, premature chromatid separation, viability, proliferation, and DNA-damage signals. A Bayesian hierarchical dose-response model would estimate the posterior probability that a compound produces meaningful rescue across several endpoints without unacceptable toxicity, share information across doses and replicates, and select follow-up experiments by expected information gain. The approach is strong because every candidate is tied to the inferred molecular defect and to measurable rescue criteria. It also builds uncertainty and stopping rules into the experiment. Its limitations are substantial: p.Asn1002Lys has not been functionally validated; the child alleles are not directly phased in trans; NMN evidence is preclinical and from a mouse context; no patient-cell rescue or drug screen has been completed; and suppression of proliferation could mimic improvement. Any lead would require functional validation, pharmacology, safety assessment, and clinical oversight before therapeutic interpretation.
